stories.headline: Door-to-door aid teams are coming. Put your papers in one envelope before the knock
stories.dek: Registration teams are headed to low-income surge-zone neighborhoods. Here's what to have ready, what renters can use as proof and how to help a neighbor get set.
body: Door-to-door aid registration teams are headed to low-income neighborhoods in the surge zone, and you can make that visit shorter by getting your papers together now.

Nueces County and FEMA announced the visits Wednesday, two days after an analysis by Coastline Public Radio and a Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi researcher found those neighborhoods received aid dollars at about half their share of residents. The county has not released a schedule.

One envelope, by the door: Your ID and the Social Security numbers of the people in your home. A working phone number, even a borrowed one, where FEMA can call you back. Insurance papers if you have coverage. Photos of the damage, printed or on your phone.

Renters: FEMA needs to see that you lived at the address. A lease works. If yours is missing, handwritten or wrong, gather backups with your name and address on them, such as a utility bill, a pay stub or a letter from your child's school or your employer.
Already applied? You don't need to start over. Put your registration number and any FEMA letters in the envelope too.
"The more you have in your hand when the team gets there, the shorter the visit and the fewer follow-up letters," said Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6.
Is it really them? As Harborline 6 reported Wednesday, team members carry federal photo ID and never charge a fee. Nobody needs your password.

"If your neighbor doesn't have a phone or a car, help them fill their envelope this weekend," said Dwayne Pruitt, spokesman for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "Then tell them a team is coming, so they open the door."
Harborline 6 will post the visit schedule on our live blog as soon as the county releases it.

stories.headline: At the Army depot, a year-end exhale after a season of leaks and long shifts
stories.dek: Corpus Christi Army Depot workers came back to soaked hangars after Rafael and had the shops at full production by Halloween. As the holiday break starts, the depot says its workforce carried it.
body: The parking lots at Corpus Christi Army Depot thin out a little more each afternoon this week as civilian mechanics start their holiday leave. Three months ago, many of those same workers were at home waiting for a phone call while crews assessed hangar roofs that Hurricane Rafael had torn open and soaked.

The depot, the military's main repair shop for helicopters, sits on Naval Air Station Corpus Christi. Before the storm it halted work and secured helicopters and components inside its hangars. Three days after landfall, it reported hangar roof damage and water intrusion and told workers to stand by.
By the end of October, the depot said it was back at full production, with parts support from DLA Distribution Corpus Christi, the Defense Logistics Agency warehouse that supplies its shops.

"Our people came back to hangars with tarps on the roofs and water on the floors, and they went to work," said Brenda Kowalczyk, a public affairs specialist at the depot. "This workforce is the mission. Nobody here forgot that, even with their own houses torn up."

The storm landed in the middle of what had been an ordinary year at the depot. In July, it was hiring helicopter mechanics, and the air station's training squadrons were on a normal summer schedule. By September, the squadrons' aircraft had flown to Fort Worth to ride out the storm; they began returning six days after landfall.
The rest of the fall brought more surprises around the station. In October, the station's backup generator failed during a power interruption. Power was restored, and the cause remains under review.
Kowalczyk said the depot's message to employees heading into the break was simple. "Rest. Hug your kids. Fix the fence you've been ignoring since September," she said. "We'll see you in January."

For many families in Flour Bluff and around the station, the holiday is the first real pause since the storm. The work on their own houses, Kowalczyk said, doesn't stop for leave. "A lot of folks are spending their vacation hanging drywall," she said. "That's this town. You fix the hangar, then you go home and fix the house."

stories.headline: Corpus Christi spill claims move to lost income as tanker owners' tab stays open
stories.dek: A claims center run for the owners of the two tankers that spilled crude during Hurricane Rafael has added lost-income claims to cleanup and property claims. No total has been released.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Three months after about 9,000 barrels of crude spilled from two tankers at an Inner Harbor terminal in Corpus Christi, the cost of the release is still being counted through a claims center run for the vessels' owners, which has widened from cleanup and property claims to lost income.

The center opened Sept. 26 for spill cleanup and property damage claims and began taking lost-income claims from fishers and shoreline businesses Nov. 16, as federal oil spill law requires. If the owners' center has not paid a claim within 90 days, the claimant can turn to the Coast Guard's National Pollution Funds Center.

The two tankers, MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay, were moored at the Rendal Terminals berth as Hurricane Rafael arrived in mid-September. Surge and wind spread sheen across about 33 square miles of Nueces and Corpus Christi bays. Fishing there remains closed by Texas Parks and Wildlife and shellfish harvesting by the Texas Department of State Health Services.

"The claims center is the owners' obligation, not the state's. Our job is making sure people know it exists and actually file," said Cole Whitaker, a spokesman for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program. "For a shrimper, that means trip logs and fuel receipts. For a shoreline business, it means the books."

Victor Lang, a spokesman for Rendal Terminals, which operates the berth, said claims tied to the vessels go through the owners' claims center. "Our position hasn't changed. Rendal is cooperating fully, and questions about the vessels belong with their owners," he said.

How the release happened is still unresolved. In September the Coast Guard said it was looking at whether someone gained unauthorized remote access to the tankers' cargo-control systems, and Brightwake Marine Systems, a vendor for those systems, said its remote-maintenance credentials were misused and cut off all remote access. Investigators have released no findings.
Neither the claims center nor the Unified Command has released a count or dollar total of claims filed so far.

stories.headline: After a long fall, base families get a holiday to catch their breath
stories.dek: From the evacuation to Fort Worth to the relief airlift and a generator scare, it has been a season. A look back, and a few reminders for the break.
body: This time last year, the biggest holiday worry around NAS Corpus Christi was whether the chapel potluck would run out of tamales. This year, plenty of our families are celebrating in houses that still smell like new drywall.

It has been a fall none of us will forget. In September, NAS Corpus Christi and NAS Kingsville flew their training aircraft to NAS Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth ahead of Hurricane Rafael. The aircraft began coming home six days after landfall, and a lot of families spent those days wondering what they would find when they got back.

In October, the station became a hub for relief, with 26 military C-17 flights and 14 civilian charters landing over ten days. During that stretch, the station's backup generator failed during a power interruption. Power was restored, and the cause is under review.

"Our sailors, civilians and families carried a heavy load this fall, and they did it while helping a whole region get back on its feet," said Lt. Marcus Hale, the station's public affairs officer. "The station is operating, the squadrons are flying, and we want everybody to take a real break."
A few reminders before you head out:
If you are traveling, make sure your command has your plans and your emergency contact information is current. September showed how fast plans can change.
If you are still working through disaster-aid paperwork, you are not alone. FEMA has urged everyone who applied for assistance to log in and confirm their direct-deposit details.
Check on the neighbor who is still living with a tarp on the roof. Bring a plate.
From all of us at Anchor & Rotor: Merry Christmas, happy holidays, and thank you for looking out for each other this year.

stories.headline: Three months after Rafael, Rosa Elizondo is still waiting on repairs
stories.dek: The home health aide and mother of three rents near the bay. Her ceiling still leaks into a bucket and her aid application is stuck, as officials promise to knock on doors.
body: The bucket in Rosa Elizondo's hallway has been there so long her kids gave it a name. "Ese es Bob," she said Friday, pointing at the plastic pail under a brown stain in the ceiling. "Bob catches the rain. Bob is the only one in this house with a steady job."

Elizondo, 38, works as a home health aide and is raising three children. She rents a duplex in one of the low-income neighborhoods near the bay that sat inside the surge zone when Hurricane Rafael came ashore Sept. 14. She doesn't own a car. Before the storm, she was among the residents without cars who waited on county buses to get out of the surge zone.
Three months later, the roof over her hallway still leaks, a back bedroom still smells of mildew, and her landlord has told her repairs are coming "after the holidays."
Her application for federal disaster aid, started in November when registration opened, has stalled. "Every time I call, it's 'pending,'" she said. "Pending, pending. I'm pending too. Ay, Dios."

Her neighborhood is the kind of place a recent analysis was about. Coastline Public Radio and a Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi researcher found that low-income neighborhoods in the surge zone received aid dollars at about half their share of residents, and that their median 911 response time was 2.1 times that of high-income areas. For weeks after the storm, residents there said they waited days for help.

On Wednesday, Nueces County and FEMA announced door-to-door aid registration in those neighborhoods. Elizondo said she will believe it when someone knocks. "If they come, Bob and I will be home," she said. "If they come."

Pastor Gloria Whitfield, who has run meals and supplies out of her church fellowship hall since before official distribution reached the neighborhood, said the knock matters more than the announcement.

"Rosa is not a case number. She's a woman with three kids and a bucket under a hole in her roof," Whitfield said. "Door to door means every door, and it means coming back when nobody answers the first time."
Elizondo said she isn't asking for much for Christmas. "A ceiling," she said. "And for Bob to retire."

stories.headline: Navy orders security review at Texas air stations, citing drone reports and channel attack
stories.dek: The review covers the Navy's air stations in Texas, including NAS Corpus Christi and NAS Kingsville. The Navy cited drone reports after Hurricane Rafael and the explosive device that closed the ship channel.
body: The Navy has ordered a security review at its air stations in Texas, including Naval Air Station Corpus Christi and Naval Air Station Kingsville, citing drone reports after Hurricane Rafael and the attack in the Corpus Christi Ship Channel this fall.
The review was announced Sunday. Navy public affairs officers said they would not discuss security measures at the stations.

"We're not going to get into specific security measures, and I'd ask people to understand why," said Lt. Marcus Hale, public affairs officer for NAS Corpus Christi. "What I can tell you is the station is operating, and a review like this is what you do after a season like the one we just had."

The drone reports date to the first nights after the storm. Two days after Rafael made landfall Sept. 14, residents near the air station began posting videos of lights hovering over it at night. The station said it was aware of the reports and working with authorities, with no impact to operations, and the FBI confirmed it was investigating. No new sightings were reported after about ten days.

The channel attack came Oct. 28, when an explosion went off beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties, injuring two crew members. The Navy said an explosive device caused the blast. Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams, working with the Coast Guard, found and rendered safe a second device near the entrance channel Nov. 5. After a 14-day closure and a full sweep, the channel reopened Nov. 11. The FBI is investigating.

"The safety of the channel and the people who work on it comes first," said Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, a public affairs officer for Navy Region Southeast. "Our teams finished a full sweep before that channel reopened. A review asks what we learned and what we do with it."
No one has publicly been identified as responsible for the drone flights or the devices.

NAS Kingsville, southwest of Corpus Christi, trains Navy jet pilots. Like NAS Corpus Christi, it flew its training aircraft to NAS Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth before the storm. Hale said families at both stations should watch official station channels for any updates.

stories.headline: Navy reviews security at Texas air stations after hurricane and port blast
stories.dek: The review follows drone reports over a Corpus Christi air station and an explosive device that shut one of the nation's busiest energy ports for two weeks.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — The Navy has ordered a security review at its air stations in Texas, citing reports of drones over Naval Air Station Corpus Christi after Hurricane Rafael and an explosive device that went off in the Corpus Christi Ship Channel in October.

The review caps a punishing fall on the Texas Gulf Coast. Rafael came ashore near Port Aransas on Sept. 14 as a Category 3 hurricane, flooding about 43 square miles across three coastal counties. Within two days, videos of lights hovering over the air station at night were circulating online. The FBI said it was investigating the reports.

On Oct. 28, an explosion beside a harbor tug near the jetties at the mouth of the ship channel injured two crew members and closed the waterway. The Navy blamed an explosive device for the blast, and its teams later found a second device and rendered it safe. The channel reopened after 14 days.

The closure mattered well beyond Texas. The Port of Corpus Christi handles about half of U.S. crude exports, and exports halted while the channel was shut. The closure also delayed the movement of a Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters and equipment through the port. The gear began sailing in November for what the Army described only as an overseas rotation.

"We take each of these incidents seriously, and we owe it to the people who live and work around our installations to look hard at what happened," said Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, a Navy Region Southeast spokeswoman.
The Navy has not publicly discussed security measures at the stations, and officials have not said who was behind the drone flights or the devices. The FBI is investigating the blast.
The review also covers Naval Air Station Kingsville, a jet training base southwest of Corpus Christi.

stories.headline: Flour Bluff man who filmed lights over air station welcomes Navy review
stories.dek: Jaime Ortega posted some of the first videos of lights over NAS Corpus Christi after Rafael. He still doesn't know what he saw, and he's glad someone is asking.
body: Jaime Ortega still has the clips. Lights hanging over NAS Corpus Christi, the nights right after Hurricane Rafael. He pulls them up again Sunday night, after the Navy says it is reviewing security at its Texas air stations.
The Navy ordered the review citing drone reports and the October attack in the ship channel. Ortega's videos were among the first posted.

"I'm an amateur. I point a camera at Jupiter," says Ortega, 42, a hobby astronomer who lives in Flour Bluff. "I never said I knew what they were. I said they weren't stars and they weren't planes. I'm glad somebody with more than a backyard telescope is looking."

In September, the station said it was aware of drone reports and working with authorities, and that operations were not affected. The FBI confirmed it was investigating. Reports of new sightings stopped after about ten days.
Ortega says he hasn't filmed anything unusual over the base since then. He still sets up his tripod on clear nights, mostly for Jupiter and Saturn, and the neighbors still ask him about it.
Ortega says his phone blew up after the videos spread. Some messages were thoughtful. Some were not.
"People wanted me to say it was aliens, or the end of the world," he says. "It was lights. That's what I filmed. I'm not going to make it bigger than it is."
The Navy isn't discussing what the review will cover. Ortega has his own advice for anyone who sees something strange near the base.
"Write down the time. Note which way it moved. Call it in," he says. "Then post it, if you want. In that order."

stories.headline: Debris and fuel contracts: where the reviews stand
stories.dek: A debris hauler and a fuel supplier hired after Rafael face a county audit, a Navy suspension and a federal inspector general review. Both deny wrongdoing.
body: Three months after Hurricane Rafael, two companies that won emergency work in its aftermath face separate reviews by the county and the Navy, and a federal inspector general is reviewing storm contracts in the region. Records reviewed by the Ledger show where each review stands.

Vantorra Restoration LLC received a $14.2 million sole-source emergency debris contract from the county on Sept. 24, ten days after landfall. The Ledger reported Dec. 1 that, according to records it obtained, the company's bills covered about 2.3 times the debris tonnage estimated by the county's own drone and satellite surveys. On Dec. 3, the county paused payments to Vantorra pending an audit.
Derek Sloane, Vantorra's managing partner, has denied overbilling. "We've been out there working around the clock since the week of the storm, and we stand behind every load," Sloane said this month.

Quellmar Fuel Partners holds a $2.1 million emergency fuel contract for Naval Air Station Corpus Christi, awarded after the station's regular supplier flooded, according to federal contract records. The station's backup generator then failed during a power interruption in October. On Nov. 28, the Navy suspended Quellmar pending a fuel quality review linked to that failure.
"All product Quellmar delivered to the station met specifications. We've said that from the start, and we expect the review to show it," said Nadia Kerr, Quellmar's operations manager.
On Dec. 7, a federal inspector general announced a review of the Coastal Bend's emergency debris and fuel contracts. The announcement did not name specific companies.
Sole-source contracts are legal in emergencies, when governments must hire quickly and cannot run a full competition. For the same reason, they tend to draw scrutiny once the emergency passes.

None of the reviews has announced findings, and neither company has been charged with a crime. The Ledger has records requests pending with the county and federal agencies and will report what they show.

stories.headline: Corpus Christi year-end: three maritime security files still open
stories.dek: Possible remote access to two tankers' cargo systems, an AIS identity anomaly and the jetty blast remain under investigation as the port heads into 2028.
body: The Corpus Christi Ship Channel has been open since Nov. 11, when it reopened after a 14-day closure and a full sweep. Three maritime security files from the fall remain without a public conclusion.

1. Cargo-system access. On Sept. 20, the Coast Guard said investigators were examining possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo-control systems of MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay, the two laden tankers at the Rendal Terminals berth from which an estimated 9,000 barrels of crude were released as Hurricane Rafael arrived. Federal cyber teams are assisting. On Sept. 22, Brightwake Marine Systems, a vendor that maintains tanker cargo systems, said its remote-maintenance credentials had been misused, revoked all remote access and said it was cooperating. No finding on the source of the access has been released.

2. AIS identity. One night in mid-October, public AIS data placed the identity of the fishing vessel FV Pelican Ridge off Port Aransas, even as the same vessel reported a position about 600 nautical miles away. Analysts later noted the spoofed identity appeared near the entrance channel two weeks before the blast. Officials have declined to comment on any link.

"A vessel identity in two places at once is consistent with spoofing. That's what the data says, and I'm not going to stretch it," said Ian McCready, an independent maritime security analyst and former Coast Guard watchstander. "Who was transmitting is still an open question. Public data alone won't answer it."

3. The jetty blast. An explosion beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties on Oct. 28 injured two crew members and closed the channel. The Navy said an explosive device caused it. Navy teams found and rendered safe a second device near the entrance channel Nov. 5. The FBI is investigating.
The Navy on Sunday ordered its Texas air stations to undergo a security review, pointing to the drone reports and the channel attack. The Navy has not discussed the review's scope.
None of the three files has a public conclusion. Gulfwater will report findings as agencies release them.

stories.headline: What the hallway beds taught: an ER nurse and an epidemiologist look back on Rafael's health toll
stories.dek: Stomach illness from the boil-water weeks has faded. Health officials say the lessons, and the slower recovery in low-income neighborhoods, should not.
body: Alyssa Cortez remembers the moment she knew the boil-water weeks were going to be bad. "It was the hallway," said Cortez, 34, a charge nurse in a Nueces County emergency department. "When you're putting stretchers in the hallway before lunch, you know the day is already lost."

Hurricane Rafael knocked out both power feeds to the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant on landfall day, damaging pumps and dropping water pressure citywide. A citywide boil-water notice followed four days later. Within days, wastewater testing picked up a norovirus signal, and by Sept. 22, ER visits for stomach illness were running about 180% above normal, with hallway beds in use.
Stomach illness visits began to ease by late September. The notice was lifted Oct. 23 after pump repairs and testing.

"People ask me about the worst case. I don't talk about patients," Cortez said. "I'll tell you about the staff. We had nurses boiling water at home for their own kids and then coming in for twelve hours. Everybody complained. Everybody came."

Dr. Anita Shah, an epidemiologist with the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District who runs its wastewater surveillance, said the testing gave the district an early warning. "The wastewater signal showed up while ER visits were still climbing. That's the value of watching it," Shah said. "It told us to get the hand-washing message out before the hallways filled."
Respiratory and skin complaints near oiled shorelines, which rose after the spill in September, were easing by early October.
Not every neighborhood recovered at the same pace. By late October, ER visits were back near normal except in low-income neighborhoods near the bay, where they were still about 40% above normal.
"When a neighborhood takes longer to come back, it's rarely one thing," Shah said. "Our job is to keep measuring until it does."
Her advice for the holidays was the same as it was in September. "Soap, a sick day at home and an early call to your doctor if you're not getting better. That list hasn't changed," she said.

stories.headline: Inside the 911 gap: researchers say the next step is finding where the time went
stories.dek: Median 911 response times in low-income surge-zone neighborhoods were 2.1 times those in high-income areas. The researcher behind the numbers says the data shows the size of the gap, not the reason.
body: In the first days after Hurricane Rafael, the Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center was taking about 2,900 calls a day, nearly ten times normal. Most came from low-lying neighborhoods near the bay.

Three months later, an analysis by Coastline Public Radio and Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi researcher Dr. Sofia Marquez found the median 911 response time in low-income neighborhoods inside the surge zone was 2.1 times that of high-income areas. The same neighborhoods received aid dollars at about half their share of residents.
The analysis measures how long help took. It does not, by itself, explain why.

"The data gives you the size of the gap. It doesn't hand you the reason," Marquez said. "Before anyone claims to have fixed this, somebody has to trace those calls and find out where the time went. That's the work a real review does."

Some background is already on the record. Before the storm, advocates warned that bus service left many households without cars in low-income neighborhoods near the bay, and they pushed for more evacuation rides. Under the mandatory evacuation, households without cars had to wait for the county's buses. After the storm, residents in those neighborhoods said they waited days for help. Marquez cautioned against treating any one of those facts as the explanation.

She does have recommendations. "Next time, response times should be tracked by neighborhood while the storm is happening, not three months later," she said. "If you can see the gap in real time, you can send people to close it. And aid outreach should start in the places with the fewest cars and the fewest phones, not end there."

The analysis compared census tracts: low-income neighborhoods inside the surge zone against the county's high-income areas. "We compared like with like as far as the data allows," Marquez said. "Every number in it can be checked, and I'd welcome people checking it."
Last week, Nueces County and FEMA announced door-to-door aid registration in low-income surge-zone neighborhoods.

"Numbers like that don't sit on a shelf," said Dwayne Pruitt, spokesman for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "Going door to door is one step. People in those neighborhoods are going to hold us to the rest, and they should."
Coastline Public Radio's tract-level maps are available on our website.

stories.headline: Relief forwarder's lesson from Rafael: the cargo was ready, the channel wasn't
stories.dek: Gulf Relief Logistics booked 40 relief containers before the storm. They landed about a month late. Its regional manager says next season's plan starts at the anchorage.
body: Terry Akins keeps a printout of the MV Gulf Provider's last position taped to the wall of his office near the port. He doesn't need it anymore. He keeps it anyway.

Akins, regional manager for Gulf Relief Logistics, booked 40 relief containers on the cargo ship five days before Hurricane Rafael made landfall. In August, relief agencies had stocked warehouses ahead of peak season, and forwarders like his had signed standby relief contracts. On paper, the Coastal Bend was ready.

Then the Coast Guard closed the port to inbound ships ahead of the storm, with 14 vessels waiting at the offshore anchorage. When the channel partly reopened Oct. 14, the anchorage backlog delayed relief cargo, including Gulf Provider. The ship finally berthed and unloaded its 40 containers Oct. 17, about a month late.

"We had the boxes stuffed, the bookings confirmed, the drayage lined up on the other end. Everything we control, we controlled," Akins said. "What you don't control is the queue at the sea buoy. Fourteen ships ahead of you and a channel that's half open, you're just a line on somebody's lineup."
Relief also came by air. Beginning Oct. 18, 26 military C-17 flights and 14 civilian charters landed at NAS Corpus Christi over ten days.
Akins said the holiday lull is when forwarders rewrite their hurricane playbooks, and his rewrite starts with the lesson that a ready cargo is only as fast as the channel.

"Next season I want a plan B that doesn't depend on one channel. Some of it pre-positioned inland before the cone even points at us, some of it ready to move by truck," he said. "Ships are cheap per box. They get real expensive when they're sitting at anchor."

He said he would also push for relief cargo to get clearer priority in any post-storm reopening, though he acknowledged that decision belongs to others. "I'm not the Coast Guard. I just know what a month late looks like to a family waiting on water," he said.
"June comes fast," Akins said. "It always does."

stories.headline: Port Aransas bait shop reopens for the holidays: 'Everything's new except me'
stories.dek: Bill Hargrove's shop near the jetties was gutted when Rafael came ashore. He's restocking for winter anglers, and he still talks about the night of the blast.
body: The Christmas lights on Hargrove Bait & Tackle are new. So is the drywall. So are most of the shelves.
"Everything in here is new except me and the cash register," says Bill Hargrove, 64. "And the register's been underwater, so it's in worse shape than I am."

Hargrove's shop sits near the Port Aransas jetties, a few miles from where Hurricane Rafael came ashore on Mustang Island on Sept. 14 as a Category 3 storm. The surge gutted it. He has ridden out storms in this spot before. This one took everything down to the studs.
He opened the doors again this month with half-stocked shelves, mostly for regulars and the winter anglers who fish the jetties.

Six weeks after landfall, Hargrove heard the explosion beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the jetties. The Navy later said an explosive device caused the blast. The channel stayed closed for 14 days before reopening Nov. 11.
"I thought Harvey was the loudest thing I'd ever hear on this island," he says. "Then that. You don't forget a sound like that. The pelicans didn't either."
Regulars have been stopping by since he reopened, he says, mostly to check on him. Some buy shrimp. Most just talk. "Half my business is conversation. Always has been," he says.
Port Aransas had a strong summer before Rafael, with bait shops and charters busy. Hargrove says he isn't counting on anything until spring break.
"Winter's for fixing things. Spring's for finding out if anybody remembers where you are," he says.
He's open through Christmas Eve and closed Christmas Day. "Even the fish get a day off," he says.

stories.headline: Christmas Eve at the fellowship hall: tamales, coats and a list of names
stories.dek: Pastor Gloria Whitfield's church hub has fed its neighborhood since before official aid arrived after Rafael. On Christmas Eve, it is still going.
body: By 9 a.m. Friday, tamales were steaming in two borrowed roasters at the back of the fellowship hall, and Pastor Gloria Whitfield was already working down a list on her penciled binder.

"This one is the widow on the next block who needs her blood-pressure medicine picked up. This is the family on the corner with the new baby," she said, tapping names. "Everybody on this list needs something, and most of them need somebody to remember they need it."

Whitfield, 59, has run meals and supplies out of her church's fellowship hall since the days after Hurricane Rafael, when church and neighborhood hubs handed out food and water before official distribution reached some neighborhoods near the bay.
Three months later, the hub is quieter, but it has not closed. On Christmas Eve, volunteers handed out tamales, donated coats and a table of wrapped toys sorted by age.

The neighborhood's wait has now been measured. Last week, Coastline Public Radio and a Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi researcher published the numbers: aid dollars reached low-income surge-zone neighborhoods at about half their share of residents. Two days after that, the county and FEMA said registration teams would go door to door there.
"I've been saying it since September, and now there's a number on it," Whitfield said. "Door to door. Good. I've got a list of doors."
Rosa Elizondo, a home health aide who rents nearby and whose hallway ceiling still leaks, as the Ledger reported last Saturday, came by with her three kids and left with tamales and a bag of oranges.
"Christmas is Christmas," Elizondo said, balancing the bag on one hip. "The roof can wait one more day. It's been waiting since September."
The volunteers, most of them neighbors, worked in shifts. Some had been coming since the week after the storm, when the hall had no power and the water came in cases.
Whitfield said the hub will stay open after the holidays. "Christmas doesn't end the need," she said. "It just makes it easier to see."

stories.headline: Navy security review: what families need to know
stories.dek: The Navy has ordered a security review at its Texas air stations, including NAS Corpus Christi and NAS Kingsville. Public affairs says daily life on the stations goes on.
body: Many of you have asked about the security review the Navy ordered Sunday at its air stations in Texas. Here is what we know, and what we don't.

What we know: The Navy ordered the review after the storm, citing drone reports and the channel attack. That covers the lights residents reported over NAS Corpus Christi in the nights after Hurricane Rafael, and the Oct. 28 explosion near the Port Aransas jetties, which the Navy later said was caused by an explosive device. The review includes NAS Kingsville.
What we don't know: the details. Anchor & Rotor does not report security measures, and the Navy has said it won't discuss them. That is how it should be.

"I know families want details. The best thing I can tell you is that the station is open, training is going on, and the people responsible for security are doing their jobs," said Lt. Marcus Hale, NAS Corpus Christi's public affairs officer. "If there's something families need to do differently, they'll hear it from us first."
Back in September, the station said it was aware of drone reports and was working with authorities, with no impact to operations. No new sightings were reported after about ten days.
A few reminders:
If you see something unusual near the station, report it to base security or local law enforcement rather than posting it first.
Check the station's official pages before sharing anything in family group chats. A lot of bad information traveled fast this fall.
Be patient at the gate. Our security forces have had a long year too.
We will share updates as public affairs releases them. Wishing all our families a peaceful Christmas Eve.

stories.headline: After a Christmas Eve shift in the ER, a charge nurse heads home for Christmas
stories.dek: Alyssa Cortez volunteered to work Christmas Eve. She walked out Saturday morning with one granola bar left and some advice for anyone heating a storm-damaged home this winter.
body: Alyssa Cortez walked out of the emergency department a little after 7 a.m. on Christmas morning, twelve hours after she walked in. One scrub pocket still held a granola bar. The other was empty.
"The one I keep for a teammate found a teammate around 3 a.m.," said Cortez, 34, a charge nurse at a Nueces County emergency department. "That's how you know it was a real shift."

Cortez volunteered weeks ago to work Christmas Eve. As always, she would not discuss individual patients. She would describe the room: a paper garland taped along the nurses' station, a plate of pan dulce a church dropped off before dark, and a waiting room that never looked like the ones she worked this fall.

The fall came at her department in waves. In the first days after Hurricane Rafael, people from neighborhoods near the oiled shorelines arrived with burning throats, watery eyes and rashes. During the boil-water notice, stomach-illness visits climbed to about 180% above normal, health officials reported at the time, and patients waited on stretchers in the hallway. By late October, officials said, visits had settled back near normal everywhere except the low-income neighborhoods near the bay, where they still ran about 40% above normal.
"A regular night. That's what I wanted for Christmas, and that's what we got," Cortez said. "After this year, regular is a present."

Her worry for the weeks ahead is the cold. Many families near the bay are still living with storm damage, roofs that leak and windows that won't close, and when the temperature drops, she said, people improvise.

"Creative heating is how I meet people at 2 in the morning," she said. "Don't heat the house with the oven. Don't bring the grill inside. Don't run a generator in the garage with the door cracked. Get a heater made for indoors, keep it away from the blankets, and turn it off when you sleep."

What readers should know: Carbon monoxide has no smell. Headaches, dizziness or nausea that ease when you step outside are a warning sign; get everyone out of the house and call 911. And if something is wrong over the holiday weekend, don't wait until Monday to call a doctor.
Cortez planned to sleep into the afternoon and then join her family for Christmas dinner. She did not sign up for New Year's Eve.
"Somebody else gets to find the eye wash," she said.

stories.headline: Christmas on the coast: a closed bait shop, a full church and presents that rode the bus
stories.dek: Bill Hargrove takes the day off at his rebuilt Port Aransas shop. Near the bay, Pastor Gloria Whitfield's church holds its Christmas service, and Rosa Elizondo's kids show off their gifts.
body: The Christmas lights are off at Hargrove Bait & Tackle in Port Aransas this morning. A sign taped to the new door reads: CLOSED CHRISTMAS DAY. GO SEE YOUR FAMILY.
Bill Hargrove, 64, drives by anyway, coffee in hand, just to look at the place.
"In September this was four walls and a smell. Now it's a store," he says. "I'm allowed to come admire it on Christmas. I'm not allowed to sell anything. Shop rules, and I wrote them."
When Rafael came ashore in September, its surge left a waterline above his head inside the shop near the jetties. He reopened it this month.

Across the bay in Corpus Christi, Pastor Gloria Whitfield's church holds its Christmas service this morning, steps from the fellowship hall it has run as a relief hub since the days after the storm, when church and neighborhood hubs handed out food and water before official help reached some neighborhoods.
"Yesterday we fed people. Today we sing," says Whitfield, 59. "After today, the doors open again. That's the whole plan."

Rosa Elizondo, 38, comes to the service with her three kids. They opened their presents at home before church. Two came from the hub's toy table this month. The third rode home with her on the bus. Elizondo doesn't have a car.
"Nobody asked how Santa got here," she says. "Good. I didn't want to explain the transfer downtown."
At home, the bucket her kids named Bob still sits in the hallway under a roof leak. Her landlord says repairs will come after the holidays.
Need help this holiday weekend? Call 2-1-1 to reach local services. Know a neighbor spending today alone? Knock on the door.

stories.headline: Rafael by port condition: the three-day sequence that closed Corpus Christi, and the ships that went to sea
stories.dek: A year-end reference for operators updating heavy-weather plans: the Coast Guard set X-Ray on Saturday, Sept. 11, closed the port to inbound traffic Sunday and to all traffic Monday. Ships at the anchorage put to sea and came back after landfall.
body: Status, Corpus Christi Ship Channel, Sunday: open to all traffic. With one hurricane season over and the next about five months out, Gulfwater sets down the sequence that closed the port ahead of Hurricane Rafael, for operators updating heavy-weather plans for 2028.

Saturday, Sept. 11: Port Condition X-Ray, meaning gale-force winds possible within 48 hours. The port stayed open. Ocean-going ships had to plan to leave or obtain approval to stay, and terminals began winding down crude loading.
Sunday, Sept. 12: Port Condition Yankee. The Coast Guard closed the port to inbound traffic. Ocean-going ships headed out, 14 inbound vessels held at the offshore anchorage, and crude exports halted.

Monday, Sept. 13: Port Condition Zulu. The ship channel closed to all traffic. Ships at the offshore anchorage put to sea to ride out the storm. Two laden tankers stayed at their Inner Harbor berth, with Coast Guard approval.

Tuesday, Sept. 14: Rafael made landfall on Mustang Island near Port Aransas around 1 a.m. as a Category 3 hurricane. Oil was reported spilling at the Inner Harbor terminal as the storm arrived; Unified Command later estimated about 9,000 barrels released from MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay.
Friday, Sept. 17: Ships that rode out the storm at sea returned to the offshore anchorage to wait. The channel stayed closed while it was surveyed and the spill was contained.
Thursday, Oct. 14: Partial reopening. Spill decontamination kept the inner channel restricted, and the anchorage backlog delayed relief cargo.

"Port conditions follow the forecast, not the calendar," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "X-Ray is the time to plan. Yankee is the time to move. By Zulu, the channel is shut, and anything still at anchor should be heading for sea room."

Operator notes. Build departure timelines from X-Ray, not Yankee. Confirm sea room and anchorage plans before inbound traffic stops. Expect the restart to depend on channel surveys and, as in 2027, on any spill response inside the port.
Not covered here: the separate closure after the Oct. 28 blast near the Port Aransas jetties, which ended when the channel reopened Nov. 11 after a full sweep.

stories.headline: Winter on the bays: spill cleanup has moved to monitoring, but the fishing closure holds
stories.dek: Three months after crude spread across Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, the shoreline work has given way to testing. Fishers are still waiting.
body: A north wind pushed whitecaps across Nueces Bay on Monday morning, and the marsh grass along the shoreline had gone winter-brown. In September, stretches of the same grass were stained black at the roots.

As Hurricane Rafael arrived, oil spilled at an Inner Harbor terminal, and the surge and wind carried it out of the ship channel into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays. The sheen covered about 33 square miles, with oil on North Beach and Portland shorelines and in the marshes. Crews deployed boom as the winds dropped, and a wildlife hotline opened.

On Oct. 28, spill cleanup moved to monitoring. The closures of fishing and shellfish harvesting in both bays, set by Texas Parks and Wildlife and the Texas Department of State Health Services, remain in place.

"Monitoring doesn't mean we walked away," said Cole Whitaker, a spokesman for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program. "It means the big shoreline work is done and the job now is testing, and testing again, before anybody reopens anything. If you see oiled wildlife, call the hotline."

Dr. Nathan Brooks, a coastal oceanographer at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi, said the timing put oil in places it normally would not reach. "The oil is sitting in marsh a normal tide never reaches, so the tide can't do much to flush it back out," Brooks said.

How long those marshes take to recover is uncertain, he said. "Marshes heal on their own clock, and winter is the slow part of it. Spring growth will tell us more than anything we can measure in January."
For commercial fishers, the closure has meant a lost season. The claims center run for the tankers' owners has taken their lost-income claims since Nov. 16.
Whitaker said the agencies' reopening decisions will follow test results. "The bays open when the data says so, not before," he said.
Along the Portland shoreline Monday, a few people walked dogs on the sand, and a pair of white pelicans worked the shallows. It looked, for a moment, like any other December.

stories.headline: FBI agents search offices of Vantorra Restoration and Quellmar Fuel Partners
stories.dek: Agents executed search warrants Monday at the two companies, which hold emergency debris and fuel contracts after Hurricane Rafael. The FBI would not say what investigators were seeking.
body: FBI agents executed search warrants Monday at the offices of Vantorra Restoration and Quellmar Fuel Partners, two companies that won emergency contracts after Hurricane Rafael and have since come under separate county and Navy reviews.
The searches came Monday, Dec. 27, the first business day after the holiday weekend.

"We can confirm FBI agents executed court-authorized search warrants today in Corpus Christi. Because this is an ongoing investigation, we have no further comment," said Mark Ellery, a spokesman for the FBI's Houston Division.

Alan Reyes, a spokesman for the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Texas, said the investigation is ongoing. "A search warrant is an investigative step. It is not a charge, and it should not be read as one," Reyes said.

Vantorra received a $14.2 million sole-source debris contract from the county Sept. 24. Records reported by the Ledger this month show the company billed for about 2.3 times the debris tonnage the county's own drone and satellite surveys estimated. The company denies overbilling, and the county has paused payments pending an audit.

Quellmar holds a $2.1 million emergency fuel contract for Naval Air Station Corpus Christi. The Navy suspended the company Nov. 28 pending a fuel quality review linked to the station's backup generator failure in October. Quellmar says its fuel meets specifications.
Separately, a federal inspector general has been reviewing the region's emergency debris and fuel contracts since Dec. 7. It is not clear whether Monday's searches are connected to that review.
Derek Sloane, Vantorra's managing partner, said "no comment" when reached by phone Monday afternoon and hung up.
In a brief written statement, Nadia Kerr, Quellmar's operations manager, said, "All product Quellmar delivered met specifications. We will respond to any questions through the proper channels."
The FBI did not say what agents were looking for, and neither company has been charged with a crime.

stories.headline: FBI searches offices of two storm contractors
stories.dek: Agents execute warrants Monday at Vantorra Restoration and Quellmar Fuel Partners. Here's what we know.
body: FBI agents execute search warrants Monday at the offices of two companies hired after Hurricane Rafael: debris hauler Vantorra Restoration and fuel supplier Quellmar Fuel Partners.
The FBI confirms the searches but isn't saying what agents are looking for.
"I can confirm the investigation, and that's all I can say today," says Mark Ellery, a spokesman for the FBI's Houston Division.
What we know about the two companies:

Vantorra holds a $14.2 million sole-source county debris contract awarded ten days after landfall. Records show it billed for about 2.3 times the debris tonnage the county's own surveys estimated. The company denies overbilling. The county has paused payments to Vantorra pending an audit.

Quellmar's emergency fuel contract with NAS Corpus Christi is worth $2.1 million. The Navy suspended the company in November pending a fuel quality review tied to the station's backup generator failure. The company says its fuel meets specifications.
What a search warrant means: A judge has to sign off on it. It lets agents look for evidence. It is not a criminal charge, and neither company has been charged.
Emergency debris and fuel contracts in the Coastal Bend are also under review by a federal inspector general. Officials have not said whether today's searches are connected to that review.
Harborline 6 has asked both companies for comment and will add their responses when we get them.

What's next: The county audit of Vantorra's billing and the Navy's fuel quality review were both under way before today. Harborline 6 will update this story as we learn more. Have a tip? Send it to our newsroom.

stories.headline: Coast Guard, CISA advisory: review vendor remote access to cargo systems
stories.dek: The joint maritime cyber advisory urges vessel operators to check how outside vendors reach cargo systems. It comes three months after the Coast Guard began examining possible remote access to two tankers in Corpus Christi.
body: The Coast Guard and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency issued a joint maritime cyber advisory Tuesday urging vessel operators to review vendor remote access to cargo systems.

Background. On Sept. 20, the Coast Guard said investigators were examining possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo-control systems of MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay, two laden tankers at the Rendal Terminals berth in the Inner Harbor. An estimated 9,000 barrels of crude were released from the two vessels as Hurricane Rafael arrived. On Sept. 22, vendor Brightwake Marine Systems, which maintains tanker cargo systems, reported that its remote-maintenance credentials had been misused and said it had revoked all remote access.

"Remote maintenance is a door into the ship. Every operator should know who holds a key, when it's used and how fast it can be taken back," said Kim Tran, a regional cybersecurity advisor with CISA. "Review vendor access. Separate cargo control from everything else. Patch what you can. Then review the access again."

"The Coast Guard urges every vessel operator to read this advisory and review vendor remote access to cargo systems," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "We will not discuss the details of any open investigation."

Operator notes. In practice, a review of vendor remote access generally starts with an inventory: which vendors hold credentials to cargo-control networks, which of those accounts are still active, and who approves a session before it opens. Operators then look at whether sessions are logged and whether credentials are revoked when a job ends.
Status. The Corpus Christi investigation remains open. Officials have not released any finding on the source of the tanker access. The ship channel is open.

stories.headline: Federal cyber advisory puts vendor access in the spotlight, three months after the Inner Harbor spill
stories.dek: The Coast Guard and CISA urged vessel operators to review vendor remote access to cargo systems. The chief of the vendor whose credentials were misused says every operator should read it.
body: Three months after oil spilled from two tankers moored at an Inner Harbor terminal as Hurricane Rafael arrived, the Coast Guard and the federal Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency on Tuesday urged vessel operators to review vendor remote access to their cargo systems.

The joint maritime cyber advisory asks operators to look hard at which outside companies can reach cargo systems from a distance, a routine arrangement that lets vendors service equipment without sending a technician aboard.

In Corpus Christi, the question is not abstract. Six days after landfall, the Coast Guard said investigators were examining possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo-control systems of MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay, which released an estimated 9,000 barrels of crude at the Rendal Terminals berth. Two days later, Brightwake Marine Systems said its remote-maintenance credentials had been misused and that it had revoked all remote access.

"We shut off every remote session in September, and we've been rebuilding how access works ever since," said Owen Pryce, Brightwake's chief executive. "I support this advisory. I'd tell every operator and every vendor in this business to read it twice. We were the ones whose credentials were misused, and I'm not going to pretend that didn't happen."

Victor Lang, a spokesman for Rendal Terminals, which operates the berth where the tankers were moored, said the company has been "cooperating fully with every agency involved" and would review the advisory with its customers.
"Questions about the vessels' own systems are for the vessel operators and the investigators," Lang said.

The spill's costs are still being counted. The claims center run for the tankers' owners has taken lost-income claims from fishers and shoreline businesses since November, and Texas Parks and Wildlife's fishing closure in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays remains in place.
The Coast Guard has said it will not discuss the details of its open investigation, and no finding on the source of the access has been released.

stories.headline: After Monday's searches: what a federal warrant means, and what comes next
stories.dek: Monday's FBI searches at two storm contractors are a step in an investigation, not a finding. Here is how the process works and which other reviews are under way.
body: FBI agents executed search warrants Monday at the offices of Vantorra Restoration and Quellmar Fuel Partners, two companies hired on emergency terms after Hurricane Rafael. Readers have asked what that means. Here is what the records and the process can tell us.

What a warrant is. A federal search warrant is signed by a judge, who must find probable cause that evidence of a crime will be found at the place to be searched. It allows agents to collect documents, devices and other material. It does not charge anyone with a crime, and it does not mean a judge has found anyone did anything wrong.

"A warrant is part of an investigation. Charges, if any are ever filed, are allegations until they are proven in court," said Alan Reyes, spokesman for the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Texas. He declined to discuss the investigation further.

What else is under way. Three other reviews predate the searches. The county paused payments to Vantorra on Dec. 3 pending an audit of its debris billing. The Navy suspended Quellmar on Nov. 28 pending a fuel quality review linked to the backup generator failure at Naval Air Station Corpus Christi. And a federal inspector general's review of emergency debris and fuel contracts across the Coastal Bend has been under way since Dec. 7.
What the companies say. Vantorra denies overbilling. Quellmar says its fuel meets specifications.

Why these contracts. Emergency rules let governments hire quickly without full competition. Vantorra's $14.2 million debris contract was sole-source, awarded ten days after landfall. Quellmar's $2.1 million fuel contract was awarded after the air station's regular supplier flooded. Records reported by the Ledger this month show Vantorra billed for about 2.3 times the debris tonnage the county's own surveys estimated.

What to watch. Investigations that involve search warrants can take months, and the public often learns little until something is filed in court. Court filings are public records, and the Ledger checks federal dockets for new filings involving companies that hold storm contracts.
We will report what the records show, and we will tell you when they show nothing new.

stories.headline: What is vendor remote access, and why are federal agencies worried about it?
stories.dek: A new Coast Guard and CISA advisory asks vessel operators to check who can reach their cargo systems from outside the ship. Here is what that means in plain terms.
body: When oil spread across Nueces Bay in September, most people on shore were thinking about the hurricane. Three months later, a federal advisory asks vessel operators a quieter question: who outside the ship can reach its cargo controls?

On Tuesday, the Coast Guard and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, known as CISA, urged vessel operators to review vendor remote access to cargo systems. Here is what that phrase means.

Cargo systems. On a tanker, cargo-control systems run the pumps and valves that move oil into and out of the tanks. Modern systems are networked, so crews can monitor and adjust them from a control station instead of walking the deck to every valve.

Vendor remote access. The companies that build and maintain those systems often service them from a distance, logging in over a network connection to diagnose problems or update software. That saves a technician a trip to the ship. It also means a set of login credentials, somewhere on land, can reach equipment on board.

"Think of it as a spare key you gave the plumber," said Dana Feld, a threat researcher at Northlight Threat Lab. "It's convenient until somebody copies it. Attackers like vendor access because it's trusted. Nobody gets alarmed when the maintenance company logs in."

Why Corpus Christi is part of the story. In September, the Coast Guard said investigators were examining possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo-control systems of the two tankers involved in the Inner Harbor spill. Brightwake Marine Systems, a vendor that maintains such systems, said its remote-maintenance credentials had been misused and revoked all remote access. Investigators have not announced a finding.

What operators can do. "The fix isn't exotic," said Kim Tran, a regional cybersecurity advisor with CISA. "Know which vendors have access. Turn it off when it isn't needed. Watch the logs, and have someone actually read them."

Feld said she would not guess who was behind the misuse in Corpus Christi. "That's for investigators to say, and they haven't said it," she said. "What I can say is the lesson doesn't depend on the answer. Every operator should know who holds a key."
For people who live along the bays, the advisory is a reminder that the spill was not only a story about weather.

stories.headline: 2027: The year Rafael came ashore, and everything that came after
stories.dek: A Category 3 hurricane, an oil spill, five weeks of boiling water, a blast at the jetties and a long fight over aid. The Ledger looks back on the year.
body: For most of the Coastal Bend, 2027 will be divided into before and after about 1 a.m. on Sept. 14, when Hurricane Rafael made landfall on Mustang Island near Port Aransas as a Category 3 storm.

September. About 11 feet of surge pushed into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays, and about 43 square miles flooded across three coastal counties. Oil spilled from two tankers moored at an Inner Harbor terminal as the storm arrived, an estimated 9,000 barrels. The O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant lost both power feeds, and four days after landfall the city issued a citywide boil-water notice. In some neighborhoods, churches and neighborhood hubs were handing out food and water before official distribution arrived.

October. Pump repairs and testing cleared the way for the city to lift the boil-water notice Oct. 23. Five days later, an explosion beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties closed the ship channel. The Navy said an explosive device caused the blast.

November. The channel reopened Nov. 11 after a 14-day closure. FEMA individual assistance registration opened Nov. 13 to long lines, and within two weeks FEMA said 410 applicant accounts had been taken over using passwords stolen elsewhere.

December. Coastline Public Radio and a Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi researcher reported that low-income surge-zone neighborhoods had received aid dollars at about half their share of residents. The county paused payments to its debris contractor pending an audit, a federal inspector general opened a review of emergency contracts, and on Dec. 27 FBI agents searched the offices of two storm contractors. This week, the Coast Guard and a federal cyber agency urged vessel operators to review vendor remote access to cargo systems.

"I've worked a few storms in this job, and this one didn't end when the wind stopped," said Dwayne Pruitt, spokesman for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "It kept finding new ways to test us. What I'll remember is the neighbors who showed up before we could."

Plenty is unfinished as the year turns. The reviews of contracts continue, the fishing closure in the bays holds, and many families in the surge zone are still waiting on repairs. The Ledger will keep reporting in 2028.

stories.headline: 2027 on the bases: evacuation, a relief hub, a generator scare and a long-delayed sailing
stories.dek: A look back at a year our installations will not forget, and the people who carried them through it.
body: Over the summer, the big news on base was hiring at the Army depot and a routine readiness inspection at NAS Corpus Christi. By December, our community had evacuated, rebuilt, hosted a relief airlift and watched the port close twice.

September. Ahead of Hurricane Rafael, NAS Corpus Christi and NAS Kingsville flew their training aircraft to NAS Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth, and Corpus Christi Army Depot halted work and secured helicopters in its hangars. The depot later reported roof damage and water intrusion. Aircraft began returning six days after landfall.

October. Over ten days, 26 military C-17 flights and 14 civilian charters landed at the station as it served as a relief hub. During that stretch, the station's backup generator failed during a power interruption; power was restored and the cause went under review. By month's end, the depot was back at full production with parts support from DLA Distribution Corpus Christi.

November. After the channel closure delayed it a second time, the Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters and equipment loaded onto a sealift ship at the port and began sailing for an overseas rotation. The Navy suspended the station's emergency fuel supplier pending a fuel quality review linked to the generator failure.
December. Citing the drone reports and the channel attack, the Navy ordered a security review at its Texas air stations.

"It was a year that asked a lot of this station and this community, and they answered every time," said Lt. Marcus Hale, the station's public affairs officer. "I'm proud of the sailors and civilians who kept this place running, and of the families who kept everything else running."

At the depot, Brenda Kowalczyk said the image she'll keep is of the workforce in the days after the storm. "People bailing water out of hangars in the morning and turning wrenches by the afternoon," she said. "That's the year in one picture."
Thank you for reading Anchor & Rotor through all of it. Happy New Year from our family to yours. Here's to a quieter 2028.

stories.headline: New year, unfinished storm business: your Rafael recovery checklist
stories.dek: Check your aid deposit details, watch for door-to-door registration, and file a spill claim if you fish or own shoreline. Here's your list for 2028.
body: Happy New Year, Coastal Bend. If Hurricane Rafael left you with paperwork, here's a short list to start 2028.

1. Check your FEMA deposit details. FEMA says 410 applicant accounts were taken over this fall after about 220,000 automated login attempts using passwords stolen from other sites. Log in, confirm your bank information, and change your password if you use it anywhere else. Affected applicants will be repaid, the agency says, and accounts now have extra verification.

2. Watch for door-to-door registration. Nueces County and FEMA announced in December that teams would register residents at their doors in low-income surge-zone neighborhoods. Ask for identification. Never give anyone your password.

3. File a spill claim if it applies to you. If you fish or own shoreline property hurt by the September oil spill, file with the claims center run for the tankers' owners. It has taken property damage claims since September and lost-income claims since November. If a claim goes unpaid for 90 days, it can go to the Coast Guard's National Pollution Funds Center.

4. Don't click the link. The city has warned about phishing emails impersonating a disaster-aid portal since the first week after landfall, and a researcher found coordinated rumor posts pointing to the same lookalike site the emails used. Type official addresses yourself.
5. Start your hurricane plan now. Hurricane season starts June 1.

"Make your plan while this one is still fresh. If you don't have a car, register for evacuation assistance through 2-1-1 well before June, not the day before a storm," says Dwayne Pruitt, spokesman for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "And write your neighbors' phone numbers on paper. Phones die."
Questions about any of this? Send them to Harborline 6 and we'll chase down answers.

stories.headline: City plans to harden water plant's power feeds; state reviews bridge wind-closure rules
stories.dek: Both power feeds to the O.N. Stevens plant failed when Rafael hit, setting off five weeks of boiling water. The city says it will harden them, and the state is reviewing when bridges close in high wind.
body: The city of Corpus Christi plans to harden the power feeds to the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant, the city's only treatment plant, after both feeds failed early in Hurricane Rafael and left residents boiling their water for five weeks, officials said Sunday.

The state, meanwhile, is reviewing its procedures for closing bridges in high wind. The Harbor Bridge and Nueces Bay Causeway closed as Rafael's winds rose and stayed shut until inspections finished, cutting Portland and North Beach off from downtown.

"We lost both feeds, and when the power goes, the pumps go. We owe it to everyone who boiled water for five weeks to make sure it doesn't happen the same way again," said Teresa Gallegos, a spokeswoman for the city water utility. "I'm sorry it took a storm to get us here. But we're here."

When Rafael made landfall Sept. 14, the plant lost both feeds, its pumps were damaged and pressure dropped citywide. A boil-water notice followed four days later. Temporary pumps limited capacity while the utility waited for replacement parts, which were delayed when the supplier's local warehouse flooded and had to ship from out of state. The parts arrived Oct. 20, and the notice was lifted Oct. 23.
In Calallen, near the plant, schoolteacher Leticia Ramos organized her neighbors' water runs during the notice. She said she is glad to hear about a plan and wants to see it on paper.

"We hauled water for five weeks. I had a spreadsheet of who needed jugs and who could drive," said Ramos, 45. "So I'd like a schedule. When does the work start, when does it finish, and who do I call when it doesn't?"

Dwayne Pruitt, spokesman for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management, said the bridge review matters to anyone who lives on the far side of the water. "When those bridges close, a big piece of this county gets cut in half," Pruitt said. "Any review that helps us plan around that is welcome."
The Ledger has asked the city for its plan documents and will report on the details as they become available.

stories.headline: State reviewing when Harbor Bridge, causeway close in high winds
stories.dek: After Rafael cut North Beach and Portland off from downtown, the state is reviewing its wind-closure procedures. A North Beach resident who got stranded has thoughts.
body: The state is reviewing its procedures for closing bridges in high winds, months after Hurricane Rafael shut the Harbor Bridge and Nueces Bay Causeway and cut North Beach and Portland off from downtown.
The bridges closed as Rafael hit in September and stayed shut until inspections finished, reopening three days after landfall.
Marcus Bell remembers every hour. Bell, 67, is a retired welder who lives on North Beach.

"Two ways off this beach, and they both close," Bell says. "I sat on my porch smelling oil off the sand and looking at that bridge. Couldn't get to the store. Couldn't have gotten to a doctor if I needed one."
He isn't asking anyone to open a bridge in a hurricane.

"I spent my whole life welding steel along that ship channel. I know what wind does to steel," he says. "I'm saying tell us the plan ahead of time, so we're not finding out by driving up to a barricade."
Bell says the closure changed how he stocks his house. "I used to keep three days of everything. Now it's a week, a full tank, and my neighbor's phone number written on paper," he says.
The review comes as the city also plans to harden the power feeds to the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant, which failed when Rafael hit.

What it means for you: The review is not a rule change yet. If you live on North Beach or in Portland, plan for the chance of being cut off from downtown for a couple of days during a storm. Keep water, medicine and a full tank on hand before the wind picks up.

stories.headline: Hardening the water plant: why the power feeds, and what the parts delay taught a supplier
stories.dek: The city's plan targets the power feeds that failed at landfall. The pump-parts supplier whose warehouse flooded says resilience is also about where spare parts sit.
body: On a cold Monday morning in Calallen, the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant hums along the Nueces River as if September never happened. The city's plan, announced Sunday, is meant to make sure the next storm doesn't silence it.

The plan is to harden the plant's power feeds. When Hurricane Rafael made landfall Sept. 14, both feeds failed early in the storm, pumps were damaged and water pressure dropped across the city. A citywide boil-water notice lasted from Sept. 18 to Oct. 23.
"Hardening the feeds comes first, because without power nothing else at that plant matters," said Teresa Gallegos, the water utility's spokeswoman.

Power was only part of the delay. After the storm, the utility said damaged pumps needed replacement parts and temporary pumps limited capacity. Then the parts were held up: the supplier's local warehouse had flooded, and the parts had to ship from out of state. They arrived Oct. 20.

Sandra Ybarra, sales manager at Delta Pumps & Controls, the supplier, said she has spent the fall thinking about where parts sit. "We had the right parts. They were in the wrong building, under water," Ybarra said. "After that, you look at a map differently. A spare that floods with the thing it's supposed to fix isn't really a spare."

She said the company is looking at keeping critical stock farther inland. "I'm still sorry about those weeks. People were boiling water and I was on the phone with freight companies," she said. "Next time I want the part on a truck before the storm makes landfall."

The city has not described which methods it will use to harden the feeds. Utilities elsewhere have buried lines, raised equipment above flood levels and added independent sources of power, but each approach comes with its own cost and timeline.
For Calallen residents, who lived closest to the plant through the five weeks of the notice, the details will matter. Gallegos said the utility will share more as the plan develops.
"We heard people loud and clear in September and October," she said. "They want to know what we're doing and when. That's fair."

stories.headline: U.S. attributes Texas tanker intrusion and ship channel explosives to a foreign government
stories.dek: Officials did not name the government. They called the intrusion into two tankers' cargo systems and the explosive devices in the Corpus Christi Ship Channel attempts to exploit Hurricane Rafael.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — U.S. officials on Tuesday attributed a cyber intrusion into two oil tankers' cargo systems and the explosive devices in the Corpus Christi Ship Channel to a foreign government, calling them attempts to exploit Hurricane Rafael. The officials did not name the government.

As the Category 3 storm arrived in September, oil spilled from two laden tankers, MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay, moored at an Inner Harbor terminal. About 9,000 barrels were released, and the surge carried the oil into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays. Within a week, the Coast Guard said investigators were examining possible unauthorized remote access to the tankers' cargo-control systems.

On Oct. 28, an explosion beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties injured two crew members and closed the channel, the gateway for about half of U.S. crude exports. The Navy said an explosive device caused the blast, and Navy teams later found and rendered safe a second device. The channel reopened after 14 days.
The closure halted crude exports, and traders braced for a long shutdown. Loadings resumed after the channel reopened Nov. 11, and ships have moved through it since.

"I'm not going to walk through the investigation," said Kim Tran, a regional cybersecurity advisor with the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. "What I'll say to every operator is what we said last week: know who has remote access to your cargo systems, and take it away when they don't need it."
"Our teams found and cleared those devices so the channel could reopen safely," said Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, a Navy Region Southeast spokeswoman. "I won't describe them."

The officials did not take questions on how they reached their conclusions, citing the ongoing investigations. The Coast Guard and CISA had already urged vessel operators in late December to review vendor remote access to cargo systems.
Officials did not describe the evidence behind the attribution.

stories.headline: 'Somebody did this': Coastal Bend reacts as U.S. blames a foreign government for tanker intrusion, channel devices
stories.dek: For shrimpers who lost a season and workers along the channel, Tuesday's attribution answers one question and leaves others open.
body: Huy Nguyen was mending a net on his boat in Aransas Pass on Tuesday when another shrimper shouted the news across the harbor.

U.S. officials had attributed the intrusion into two tankers' cargo systems and the explosive devices in the ship channel to a foreign government they did not name, calling them attempts to exploit Hurricane Rafael.

"Since September, everybody says 'under investigation,'" said Nguyen, 51, a second-generation shrimper whose season was lost to the spill closure. "Now they say somebody did this. OK. Somebody did this. My nets are still dry."

The oil spilled from MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay at the Rendal Terminals berth as Rafael arrived in September, an estimated 9,000 barrels. Surge and wind carried it into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, and Texas Parks and Wildlife and the state health department closed fishing and shellfish harvesting in both. By Sept. 20, six days after landfall, investigators were examining possible unauthorized remote access to the tankers' cargo-control systems, the Coast Guard said.

Victor Lang, a spokesman for Rendal Terminals, said the company "has cooperated fully with every agency from the first day." He declined to discuss the investigation. "Today's announcement is the government's to explain. We'll leave it to them to say more," Lang said.

Cole Whitaker, spokesman for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program, said the attribution does not change the work on the water. Cleanup moved to monitoring in October, and testing continues. "Whoever was responsible, the oil was in our bays, and the job is the same: monitor, keep testing and get the bays ready to reopen when it's safe," Whitaker said.

The attribution also covered the explosive devices in the channel, including the one behind the Oct. 28 blast beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties, which injured two crew members and closed the channel for 14 days.
Nguyen filed a lost-income claim in November, after the tanker owners' claims center began accepting them. He said Tuesday's news doesn't change his math.
"Boat payment is the same. Fuel is the same. Claim is still pending," he said. "Tell me who did it, fine. I still want to know when I can fish."

stories.headline: Attribution covers tanker intrusion and channel devices; Coast Guard says channel open
stories.dek: Officials named neither the foreign government nor its methods. The Coast Guard points operators back to last week's advisory on vendor remote access.
body: U.S. officials on Tuesday attributed the intrusion into the cargo-control systems of MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay, and the explosive devices in the Corpus Christi Ship Channel, to a foreign government they did not name. Officials called the incidents attempts to exploit Hurricane Rafael.

Scope. The attribution covers two incidents. The first is the intrusion affecting the two laden tankers at the Rendal Terminals berth, from which an estimated 9,000 barrels of crude were released as the storm arrived in September. The second is the devices off the entrance channel: one detonated beside the tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties Oct. 28, and Navy teams rendered a second safe Nov. 5.

Investigation history. The cyber thread dates to Sept. 20, when the Coast Guard first said it was looking into possible unauthorized remote access to the tankers' cargo-control systems with help from federal cyber teams. On Oct. 30, the Navy said the blast was caused by an explosive device; Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams searched the channel with the Coast Guard, and the FBI is investigating.
Port condition. Open. The channel returned to service Nov. 11 after a full sweep ended its 14-day closure.

"The channel is open. Today's announcement does not change port conditions," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "The Coast Guard will not comment on the details of the attribution."

Operator guidance. The Dec. 28 joint maritime cyber advisory from the Coast Guard and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency tells vessel operators to review vendor remote access to cargo systems. Ruiz said operators should treat it as current. "If you have not completed that review, complete it," she said.
Not released. Officials did not identify the government, describe the evidence or say how the intrusion was carried out. Gulfwater does not speculate on attribution beyond what officials state.

stories.headline: At the jetties, a tug captain and a bait shop owner react: 'I'd like a name'
stories.dek: Capt. Ray Dupree's tug was beside the October blast. Bill Hargrove heard it from home. Both say Tuesday's attribution is a start.
body: Capt. Ray Dupree has worked the Corpus Christi Ship Channel for 30 years. On Tuesday, he learns who the government says put explosives in it. Sort of.
U.S. officials attribute the explosive devices in the channel, along with the cyber intrusion into two tankers during Hurricane Rafael, to a foreign government. They don't say which one.

"A foreign government. That's what I got," says Dupree, 56, master of the harbor tug Corrin Bay, which was damaged in the Oct. 28 blast near the Port Aransas jetties. "My deckhand got hurt. My boat got hurt. I'd like a name. But I've been on the water long enough to know you don't always get one."
