Dupree says the blast came off the tug's port bow. He doesn't like describing it again. "I've told it enough times," he says. "I'd rather talk about my crew."
Two crew members were hurt in the blast. One of them, deckhand Eddie Fontenot, told reporters in December he was recovering.
Bill Hargrove, who owns Hargrove Bait & Tackle near the jetties, heard the explosion from home that night.
"Every old-timer on this island had a theory. Gas line, old ordnance, sea monster," says Hargrove, 64. "Turns out it was worse than the sea monster."
Hargrove says customers have been asking about it all afternoon.
The Navy said an explosive device caused the blast, and Navy teams later found a second one. Once the full sweep was done, the channel reopened Nov. 11, two weeks after the blast.
Dupree says his crew has always watched the water at the jetties.
"We always did," he says. "Now we know why."

stories.headline: What Tuesday's attribution says, and what it leaves out
stories.dek: Officials blamed a foreign government they did not name for the tanker intrusion and the channel devices. Here is what was said, what wasn't, and what comes next.
body: On Wednesday morning, ships moved past the Port Aransas jetties the way they have since mid-November, through water that Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams spent two weeks searching this fall. The question hanging over that water now has part of an answer.

On Tuesday, U.S. officials attributed two things to a foreign government they did not name: the intrusion into two tankers' cargo systems as Hurricane Rafael arrived in September, and the explosive devices in the Corpus Christi Ship Channel. They called both attempts to exploit the hurricane.

The intrusion is the one the Coast Guard first described six days after landfall, when it said investigators were looking into possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo systems of two tankers, MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay. The tankers released an estimated 9,000 barrels of crude at an Inner Harbor berth. There were two devices: one that exploded beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the jetties Oct. 28, injuring two crew members, and a second that Navy teams found near the entrance channel and rendered safe in early November.

What officials did not say is just as important. They did not name the government, describe their evidence or say whether anyone will be charged, and they did not tie the attribution to any other event.
"We can confirm the investigation is continuing. We have no further comment," said Mark Ellery, a spokesman for the FBI's Houston Division.
An attribution is a government's public judgment about who is responsible. It is not a court case, and the evidence behind it is often kept out of public view.

For the companies that run ships and terminals, the practical advice has not changed, said Kim Tran, a regional cybersecurity advisor with the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. "Who did it matters to investigators. For an operator, the job is the same either way: know every vendor that can reach your cargo systems remotely, and be able to cut them off fast," she said. Last week, the Coast Guard and CISA issued an advisory urging vessel operators to review that access.

Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, a Navy Region Southeast spokeswoman, said the teams that swept the channel did their work long before Tuesday. "The channel was cleared in November, and it's open," she said. "Who put the devices there is a question for investigators. Keeping the water safe is ours."

For the tug crews, line handlers and pilots who lost two weeks of work in the fall, Tuesday's announcement answers what happened more than who did it. Coastline Public Radio will report what officials release as the investigation continues.

stories.headline: Attribution puts Gulf export security on traders' radar
stories.dek: U.S. officials blamed a foreign government for the channel devices that halted Corpus Christi crude exports for 14 days. Analysts say security now sits beside weather in shipping risk.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — U.S. officials' attribution of the Corpus Christi ship channel devices and a tanker cyber intrusion to a foreign government adds a new line to the risk ledger for the largest U.S. crude export gateway, analysts said Wednesday.

The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports. Exports halted after an Oct. 28 explosion near the Port Aransas jetties, which the Navy said was caused by an explosive device, and resumed when the channel reopened Nov. 11 after 14 days.

"Until yesterday, the market could file the blast as a one-off with no name on it. Now it has a category: a government trying to exploit a hurricane," said Grace Holloway of Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "That doesn't move a barrel today. It moves how buyers and insurers think about the next storm."

Holloway said the questions from buyers will change. "It used to be, how fast does the channel reopen after a hurricane. Now it's also, who's watching the channel while everyone's watching the storm," she said.

The channel's two closures this fall came for different reasons, Holloway noted: Hurricane Rafael in September, the blast in October. "One of those you could see coming on a forecast map. The other one, officials are now telling us, was somebody trying to take advantage of the first," she said.

Officials called the intrusion and the devices attempts to exploit Hurricane Rafael but did not name the government. That came a week after the Coast Guard and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency told vessel operators to review the remote access their vendors have to cargo systems.

Holloway said she expects tanker operators and charterers to ask more questions about vendor access and channel security before booking Gulf Coast cargoes for the summer. "None of it changes the barrels. It changes the paperwork," she said.
The channel remains open.

stories.headline: Opinion: The storm was natural. The port's defenses have to account for what wasn't
stories.dek: An opinion column. Federal officials now say a foreign government tried to exploit Rafael. The port and its partners should plan for the next hurricane as a security event, too.
body: For four months, the story of Hurricane Rafael on the water has been told in the language of weather: surge heights, wind speeds, the bad luck of two loaded tankers at the berth when the storm came in. On Tuesday, federal officials changed the vocabulary.

U.S. officials attributed the intrusion into the tankers' cargo systems and the explosive devices in the ship channel to a foreign government, which they did not name, and called them attempts to exploit the hurricane. Every port authority, terminal operator and shipping line on the Gulf should read that sentence twice.

Corpus Christi handles about half of U.S. crude exports. For 14 days this fall, after the blast at the jetties, it handled none. A hurricane will always close the channel for a while. The lesson of Rafael is that a hurricane can also be cover.

Some of the work has started. Last week, the Coast Guard and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency told vessel operators to take a hard look at which vendors can reach their cargo systems remotely. In December, the Navy ordered a security review at its Texas air stations. Those are good first steps, and they are mostly federal.

What is missing is a local plan that treats the next storm as both a weather event and a security event. When the next hurricane closes the channel, who keeps watch on the water while no ships can move? Who checks which outside vendors can log into ships at the berth before the wind arrives? Who tells residents, quickly and plainly, what is known and what is not?

The port, the Coast Guard and the companies that use the channel should answer those questions together, in public, before June. They do not need to publish anything that would help an adversary. They do need to show the rest of us that someone owns the problem.
The next storm will not wait for the after-action report.
Grant Okafor covers the port and business for the Bayside Ledger. This column reflects his views.

stories.headline: Federal filing: storm debris and fuel contractors share offshore owner; accounts got $3.9 million in diverted aid
stories.dek: A civil forfeiture filing says Vantorra Restoration and Quellmar Fuel Partners are both owned by Brannoch Maritime Holdings, an offshore company, and that bank accounts tied to the firms received about $3.9 million in diverted disaster aid.
body: Two companies hired on emergency terms after Hurricane Rafael share an owner, an offshore company called Brannoch Maritime Holdings, and bank accounts tied to the firms received about $3.9 million in diverted disaster aid, according to a federal civil forfeiture filing made public Thursday.
The filing names debris hauler Vantorra Restoration LLC and fuel supplier Quellmar Fuel Partners. It lists Brannoch's director as L. Marrick.
A civil forfeiture case is brought against money or property, not against a person, and it is not a criminal charge. The filing's claims are allegations that have not been proven in court.

"The filing speaks for itself. Its claims are allegations, and the owners of the property will have the opportunity to respond in court," said Alan Reyes, spokesman for the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Texas. He declined to comment on anything not described in the filing.

Both firms have been under scrutiny for months. The county awarded Vantorra a $14.2 million sole-source debris contract on Sept. 24. Records reported by the Ledger in December show it billed for about 2.3 times the debris tonnage the county's own surveys estimated, which the company denies; the county paused payments pending an audit. Quellmar was awarded a $2.1 million contract to supply emergency fuel to Naval Air Station Corpus Christi. The Navy suspended it in November pending a fuel quality review, and the company says its fuel meets specifications. A federal inspector general opened a review of emergency debris and fuel contracts Dec. 7, and FBI agents searched both companies' offices on Dec. 27.

The filing describes the $3.9 million as diverted disaster aid but does not say how it was diverted, and Reyes would not elaborate. Separately, in November, FEMA said 410 applicant accounts had been taken over after about 220,000 automated login attempts and their deposit details changed, and that affected applicants would be repaid.

Derek Sloane, Vantorra's managing partner, said Thursday that the company "did the work we were hired to do" and would respond through its attorneys. He did not answer questions about the company's ownership.
Nadia Kerr, Quellmar's operations manager, said in a statement that "all product Quellmar delivered met specifications" and that the company would respond in court.

stories.headline: Diverted aid named in federal filing: what FEMA applicants should check now
stories.dek: A federal filing says about $3.9 million in diverted disaster aid went to accounts tied to two storm contractors. FEMA says applicants whose accounts were taken over will be repaid.
body: A federal civil forfeiture filing made public Thursday says bank accounts tied to two storm contractors, Vantorra Restoration and Quellmar Fuel Partners, received about $3.9 million in diverted disaster aid. The filing does not say how the aid was diverted. If you applied for FEMA aid, here's what to know.

What happened to applicant accounts: In November, some aid applicants said their direct-deposit details had been changed without their knowledge. FEMA confirmed unauthorized access to some accounts, then said 410 accounts were taken over after about 220,000 automated login attempts using passwords stolen elsewhere.
Will you be repaid? FEMA has said affected applicants will be repaid.
"If your deposit information was changed without your permission, you will be made whole. That has not changed," says Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer with FEMA Region 6.
What to do right now: Log in and confirm your direct-deposit information. Use the extra verification FEMA added. If your password is used on any other site, change it.

Already reported a problem? Keep your confirmation number and any letters FEMA sends, and write down the date you reported it. Still waiting on a first payment? Check your application status and make sure your phone number and address are current.
Does the filing mean someone was charged? No. A civil forfeiture case targets money or property, not people, and its claims are allegations. The companies can contest it in court.

Who are the companies? Vantorra holds a county debris contract. Quellmar supplied emergency fuel to NAS Corpus Christi. The filing says both are owned by an offshore company, Brannoch Maritime Holdings.
"Never give your password to anyone who calls, texts or knocks. We will not ask for it," Ostrander says.

stories.headline: In the neighborhoods that got the least, news of $3.9 million in diverted aid lands hard
stories.dek: Low-income surge-zone neighborhoods received aid at about half their share of residents. Now a federal filing says millions in disaster aid were diverted to accounts tied to two storm contractors.
body: Pastor Gloria Whitfield read the news on her phone in the fellowship hall Thursday afternoon, between a delivery of diapers and a call about a leaking roof. Then she read it again, out loud, to nobody in particular.

A federal civil forfeiture filing says bank accounts tied to two companies hired after Hurricane Rafael, Vantorra Restoration and Quellmar Fuel Partners, received about $3.9 million in diverted disaster aid. According to the filing, an offshore company, Brannoch Maritime Holdings, owns both firms. A civil forfeiture case is brought against money, not people; it is not a criminal charge, and its claims have not been proven in court.

"Three point nine million dollars," Whitfield said. "I have families on my list who got nothing, or half of nothing. And the filing says disaster money ended up in accounts tied to contractors? Lord, give me patience, because I am all out."

Whitfield's neighborhood is one of the low-income surge-zone neighborhoods that, according to a December analysis by Coastline Public Radio and Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi researcher Dr. Sofia Marquez, received aid dollars at about half their share of residents. Her church hub was handing out food and water before official distribution arrived after the storm. In mid-December, the county and FEMA announced door-to-door aid registration in those neighborhoods.

Marquez cautioned against blending the two stories. "These are separate problems, and it matters not to blur them," she said. "The gap we measured is about who got reached in the first place. Diverted aid, as the filing describes it, is about where money went. But for a family, both end the same way: the help doesn't arrive."

Marquez said her team plans to keep tracking aid by tract once door-to-door registration gets under way. "If outreach works, the numbers should move. If they don't move, that tells you something too," she said.
Separately, FEMA said in November that 410 applicant accounts had been taken over and that affected applicants would be repaid.
Whitfield said she would keep doing what she has done since September, and she wants the door-to-door teams to start soon.
"The money can sort itself out in court," she said. "The roof on the next block can't wait for a judge."

stories.headline: Fishing grounds partly reopen after testing as spill claims reach about 4,200
stories.dek: Part of the bay waters closed since the September oil spill reopened after testing. Shrimpers say it's a start, and the claims keep coming.
body: Part of the fishing grounds closed since oil spread across Nueces and Corpus Christi bays in September reopened after testing, and about 4,200 spill damage claims have been filed by fishers and shoreline owners, officials said Friday.

Texas Parks and Wildlife closed fishing and the Texas Department of State Health Services closed shellfish harvesting in both bays four days after Hurricane Rafael made landfall, after surge and wind carried crude spilled at an Inner Harbor terminal across about 33 square miles of water. The fishing closure was extended in October, and spill cleanup moved to monitoring at the end of that month.

"The agencies reopened what the testing supports, and nothing more," said Cole Whitaker, spokesman for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program. "Areas that are still closed stay closed until their results say otherwise. Check the current closure maps before you go out."

Since September the tanker owners' claims center has taken property damage claims, and since Nov. 16 it has also taken lost-income claims from fishers and shoreline businesses. Whitaker urged anyone who lost income or property to the spill to file and to keep records. "If you haven't filed and you think you're owed, file. If you filed, keep your receipts and your trip logs," he said.
In Aransas Pass, shrimper Huy Nguyen said the news was welcome and not enough.

"Part of the bay is part of a living," said Nguyen, 51, a second-generation shrimper whose boat survived the storm but whose season did not. "I filed my claim in November. I'm still paying on the boat. Fuel is not cheaper because the oil was in the water."

Nguyen said he planned to run his boat out to look at the reopened water before deciding what to do with the rest of the winter. He has fished these bays most of his life, and he said he wanted to see the water for himself before trusting it.
"The test says it's OK. I believe the test," he said. "I still want to look."
He counted it out the way he counts most things, in numbers.
"Four thousand two hundred people waiting. I'm one," he said. "We'll see who gets paid first."

stories.headline: Station's suspended emergency fuel supplier named in federal court filing
stories.dek: A civil forfeiture filing says Quellmar Fuel Partners, which the Navy suspended in November, shares an offshore owner with a county debris contractor.
body: Quellmar Fuel Partners, the company that supplied emergency fuel to NAS Corpus Christi after Hurricane Rafael, is named in a federal civil forfeiture filing made public Thursday.

The filing says Quellmar and Vantorra Restoration, a county debris contractor, share an owner, Brannoch Maritime Holdings, an offshore company whose listed director is L. Marrick. It also says bank accounts tied to the firms received about $3.9 million in diverted disaster aid. A civil forfeiture case is brought against money or property, not people, and its claims are allegations, not criminal charges.

Quellmar received a $2.1 million emergency fuel contract for the station after the station's regular supplier flooded. The station's backup generator failed during an October power interruption, and the Navy suspended Quellmar on Nov. 28 pending a fuel quality review tied to that failure. The company has said its fuel meets specifications. FBI agents searched Quellmar's offices on Dec. 27.

"We're aware of the filing. It's a court matter, so I'll let the filing speak for itself," said Lt. Marcus Hale, the station's public affairs officer. "What families should know is that the station has power, the squadrons are flying, and base services are not affected."
Hale declined to discuss the status of the Navy's fuel quality review.

For families who have followed this story since the generator outage in October, the filing is the clearest public picture yet of who owns the company. It does not answer every question, and Anchor & Rotor will not speculate beyond what the filing and public affairs say.
If you have questions about base services, check the station's official channels. Anchor & Rotor will pass along any update from public affairs, and we will follow the case as it moves through court.

stories.headline: From a sole-source award to a forfeiture filing: the paper trail on two storm contractors
stories.dek: In less than four months, two companies hired after Rafael went from emergency contracts to a federal filing naming a shared offshore owner. A timeline from the public record.
body: Four months ago, few people in the Coastal Bend had heard of Vantorra Restoration or Quellmar Fuel Partners. On Thursday, a federal civil forfeiture filing said both share an owner, Brannoch Maritime Holdings, an offshore company whose listed director is L. Marrick, and that about $3.9 million in diverted disaster aid landed in bank accounts tied to the firms. Here is how the public record got there.
Sept. 24: Ten days after landfall, the county awards Vantorra a $14.2 million sole-source emergency debris contract.
Oct. 4: Federal contract records show a $2.1 million emergency fuel contract for Naval Air Station Corpus Christi to Quellmar, after the station's regular supplier flooded.
Oct. 25: During a power interruption, the station's backup generator fails, the station says. Power is restored, and the cause goes under review.

Nov. 17 to Nov. 24: In a separate FEMA matter, aid applicants report deposit details changed without their knowledge. FEMA confirms unauthorized access, then says 410 accounts were taken over after about 220,000 automated login attempts. FEMA says affected applicants will be repaid.
Nov. 28: Quellmar is suspended by the Navy, pending a fuel quality review tied to the generator failure. The company says its fuel meets specifications.
Dec. 1: Records show Vantorra billed for about 2.3 times the debris tonnage the county's own drone and satellite surveys estimated. Vantorra managing partner Derek Sloane denies overbilling.
Dec. 3: Payments to Vantorra are put on hold while the county audits its billing.
Dec. 7: Emergency debris and fuel contracts across the Coastal Bend come under a federal inspector general's review.
Dec. 27: FBI agents execute search warrants at both companies' offices.

Jan. 6: The forfeiture filing names the shared owner and the diverted aid. Vantorra says it will respond through its attorneys; Quellmar operations manager Nadia Kerr says the company will respond in court.
A civil forfeiture case targets money or property, not people, and the filing's claims have not been proven in court. No one has been criminally charged in the public record so far.

What the public record does not yet show: how the aid was diverted, whether anyone will face criminal charges, and what the county audit and the inspector general's review will find. The Ledger will keep reading the filings.

stories.headline: Opinion: Finish the door-to-door work before the last chapter of Rafael is written
stories.dek: An opinion column. A federal filing says millions in disaster aid were diverted. The neighborhoods that got the least still need someone to knock.
body: I've spent four months in the neighborhoods near the bay where the water came up highest and help came last. I've watched people fill out the same form three times, sit on hold through a lunch break, and wait months on a ceiling that dripped into a bucket.

In December, an analysis by Coastline Public Radio and a Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi researcher put a number on what those residents had been telling us since September: low-income surge-zone neighborhoods received aid dollars at about half their share of residents, and their median 911 response time was 2.1 times that of high-income areas.

This week, a federal civil forfeiture filing put a number on something else: about $3.9 million in diverted disaster aid that, the filing says, went to bank accounts tied to two storm contractors. Those claims have not been proven in court, and the companies are entitled to answer them. But the figure lands hard in neighborhoods that got about half their share.

In December, the county and FEMA promised door-to-door registration in those neighborhoods. That promise is the most useful thing to come out of this review season. It is also the easiest to let slide once the headlines move on.

Here is what finishing it looks like. Knock on every door, and go back to the ones that don't answer. Send people who speak Spanish. Leave paper, not just a link. Publish how many households were reached, by neighborhood, every two weeks until the job is done. And make sure every applicant whose deposit details were hijacked is repaid, as FEMA has promised.
The church halls that fed these neighborhoods before the trucks came are still open. They should not have to be the plan.
Marisol Treviño is the Ledger's city and disaster reporter. This column reflects her views.

stories.headline: Port of Corpus Christi starts 2028 with an open channel and a longer to-do list
stories.dek: Exports are flowing after two closures in a single fall. The port's spokesman says resilience and security will shape the year.
body: A loaded tanker slid under the Harbor Bridge on Monday morning, trailed by gulls, the kind of sight that drew no attention a year ago and drew a few phone cameras this fall, when the channel sat empty for weeks.

The Port of Corpus Christi enters 2028 with its channel open, exports flowing and a list of lessons from a fall that closed it twice: first for Hurricane Rafael in September, then for 14 days after an explosive device went off beside a tug near the Port Aransas jetties in October.

Since then, the channel reopened Nov. 11 and exports resumed. Vessel operators were told by the Coast Guard and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency to review vendor remote access to cargo systems. And last week, U.S. officials attributed the channel devices and an intrusion into two tankers' cargo systems to a foreign government they did not name.

"The channel is open, the docks are working and our customers are shipping," said Javier Salinas, spokesman for the Port of Corpus Christi. "This fall taught us that being ready for hurricanes isn't the whole job anymore. We'll keep working with the Coast Guard and our federal partners on the rest of it."
Salinas declined to discuss specific security measures.

The stakes reach well beyond Nueces County. Before the storm, the port was handling about half of U.S. crude exports. When the channel closed, those exports stopped. The partial reopening in October also left relief cargo waiting in an anchorage backlog.

What to watch this year: whether vessel operators finish the vendor-access reviews federal agencies have urged; how the port and its tenants plan for the next storm-season closure; and whether lessons from the anchorage backlog turn into new procedures before June.
"We had a hard fall," Salinas said. "We'd like a boring summer."

stories.headline: Rafael, four months on: four neighbors, four kinds of waiting
stories.dek: A home health aide, a schoolteacher, a shrimper and a bait shop owner take stock as rebuilding continues and reviews of water, aid, port security and contracting go on.
body: Four months after Hurricane Rafael came ashore on Mustang Island, the Coastal Bend is still rebuilding, and the reviews are still running: of the water system, of who got aid, of port security, of emergency contracts. For the people the Ledger has followed since the storm, recovery looks different on every street.

Near the bay. Rosa Elizondo, 38, a home health aide and mother of three, finally has a ceiling. Her landlord patched the hallway leak the first week of January, she said. Her aid application is still pending, and she is still waiting for the door-to-door teams the county and FEMA announced in December to reach her street. "Bob is retired," she said of the bucket that caught the drip for months. "Now I need FEMA to un-pend me. They're slow, but I'm stubborn."

In Calallen. Leticia Ramos, 45, the schoolteacher who organized her neighbors' water runs during the five-week boil-water notice, still keeps her spreadsheet. "I deleted the jug column. I kept the phone numbers," she said. The city plans to harden the water plant's power feeds; Ramos wants dates. "A plan without a deadline is a wish," she said.

In Aransas Pass. Shrimper Huy Nguyen, 51, saw part of the fishing grounds reopen last week after testing. His is one of about 4,200 spill damage claims filed so far. "Some water open. No check yet. Boat payment every month," he said.

In Port Aransas. Bill Hargrove, 64, has his bait shop near the jetties stocked again, mostly. "Two-thirds of a store and all of the jokes," he said. He is counting the weeks to spring break. "If the fish come back and the tourists come back, I'll forgive this whole year. Probably."
The analysis that showed low-income surge-zone neighborhoods like Elizondo's got aid dollars at about half their share of residents is part of what the reviews are now weighing.
Elizondo said the day she is waiting for isn't on a calendar. "When my kids stop asking if the water is coming back," she said, "that's when it's over."

stories.headline: Four months after Rafael, the reviews are under way. A pastor and a deckhand say what they'd ask
stories.dek: Water, aid equity, port security and contracting are all under review. Two people who lived through the storm's hardest moments say what reviewers should hear.
body: The fellowship hall smells like coffee and bleach on a Tuesday morning in January. Pastor Gloria Whitfield is sorting donated blankets into piles by size, the same way she sorted cases of water in September.

Four months after Hurricane Rafael, rebuilding continues across the Coastal Bend, and reviews of water, aid equity, port security and contracting are under way. Some have already produced news. The city plans to harden the water plant's power feeds. The Coast Guard and a federal cyber agency issued an advisory on vendor access to cargo systems. The Navy put its Texas air stations under a security review.

For Whitfield, the review that matters most is about who got help. Low-income surge-zone neighborhoods like hers received aid dollars at about half their share of residents, according to a December analysis by Coastline Public Radio and a Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi researcher. The county and FEMA have promised door-to-door registration there. Last week, a federal civil forfeiture filing said about $3.9 million in diverted disaster aid went to accounts tied to two storm contractors; its claims have not been proven in court.
"I want the reviewers to come sit in this hall for one morning," Whitfield said. "Not to take a picture. To answer the door when somebody knocks with a problem. Then write the report."

Down the coast, Eddie Fontenot has a different question. The 29-year-old deckhand broke his arm and suffered a concussion when an explosive device went off beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties on Oct. 28. Last week, U.S. officials said a foreign government, which they did not name, was behind both the channel devices and an intrusion into two tankers' cargo systems.
"I'm grateful I'm here. Grateful for the guys who got me out," Fontenot said. "But I want somebody to tell me how they keep it from happening to the next guy. That's my whole question."
His arm is out of the cast, and he said he has been cleared to go back to work. "Yeah. I'm going back," he said. "It's what I do."
Whitfield said four months is too soon for anyone to call the job finished. "Ask me again at a year," she said. "Ask me again at two."
